title: Sequences as State Machines with CASE
oneLiner: How PLC programs run step-by-step processes: one state variable, a CASE that moves between states, timers per state, outputs derived from the state, with a simulated tank and a conveyor sorter.
keyTakeaway: Keep the current step in one INT, let a CASE decide each step's transitions, handle stop and faults above it, give timed steps their own timers, and write the outputs from the state in one place afterwards.
explanation:
Most machines do things in order: fill, then heat, then drain; clamp, then drill, then release. Writing a sequence as a pile of separate latched bits works for three steps and becomes unreadable at ten. The standard approach is a state machine: one variable holds which step the machine is in, and a CASE statement says, for each step, which conditions move it on to the next.

A state machine, also called a sequencer, has a fixed set of states, exactly one of which is active at a time, and transitions between them triggered by conditions such as a sensor, a timer or a button. In ST it is an INT variable and a CASE on it. The outputs are then worked out from the state, each in one place, so a step can't forget to switch something off. Stop and fault handling sit above the CASE so they apply in every state.

IEC 61131-3's Sequential Function Chart language draws exactly this structure as boxes and lines, and some teams use it for sequences. Writing it in ST teaches the same thinking and works in any tool. Below are a tank sequence (fill, mix, drain) running against a simulated tank and a conveyor that sorts metal parts; the exercises are a traffic light and a conveyor jam detector.
